outline: What an API is and why it matters
Analogy: API as a connector between requests and models
API keys for authentication and access control
How applications send requests and receive AI-generated responses

slides.title: Title Slide
slides.narration: Welcome to this Spoken Tutorial on Understanding **APIs**.

slides.title: Learning Objectives Slide
slides.narration:
In this tutorial, you will learn,
	• What an **API** is and its fundamental purpose.
	• How **APIs** integrate **AI** models into applications.
	• About components in sending and receiving **API** requests.
	• The importance of **API** keys for authentication.

slides.title: System Requirements Slide
slides.narration: Here I am using a browser on a computer or mobile.

slides.title: Pre-requisite Slide
slides.narration:
To follow this tutorial, you should have a basic understanding of web applications and data transfer.
No coding needed.

slides.title: Understanding APIs
slides.narration:
Let's begin our journey into understanding **APIs**.
This section will introduce you to their fundamental role.

slides.title: Defining an API
slides.narration:
What exactly is an **API**?
Imagine two different software applications needing to communicate.
An **API** acts as a messenger, allowing them to talk.
It's a software intermediary that connects them.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing two different software applications communicating via an API acting as a messenger or intermediary.

slides.title: Why APIs are Crucial for AI
slides.narration:
Why are **APIs** so crucial for **AI**?
They enable seamless integration of powerful **AI** models.
This expands the capabilities of many applications.
Think of it as adding smart features to any software.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing an AI model seamlessly integrating into an application, enhancing its capabilities with smart features.

slides.title: API as a Bridge
slides.narration:
Let's visualize an **API**.
It's like a bridge connecting your application to an **AI** model.
Or, imagine a waiter taking your order to the kitchen.
The **API** takes your application's request to the **AI** model.
Then it brings the processed response back.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration of an API as a bridge connecting an application to an AI model, or a waiter taking an order to a kitchen and bringing back food.

slides.title: The Request-Response Cycle
slides.narration:
How does this communication happen?
It follows a simple request-response cycle.
Your application sends a request to the **API**.
The **API** then sends back a structured response.
This is the basic flow for all **API** interactions.
slides.image_prompt: Diagram illustrating a clear request-response cycle between an application and an API, showing data flow.

slides.title: Introduction to API Keys
slides.narration:
With that understanding, let's talk about **API** keys.
These are unique identifiers, like a digital key.
They authenticate users and control access to **API** services.
Without a valid key, access is often denied.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration of a digital key unlocking access to secure API services, representing an API key.

slides.title: Security and Usage Management
slides.narration:
Why are **API** keys important?
They ensure secure access to valuable services.
They also track how much an **API** is being used.
This helps manage consumption limits and prevent misuse.
It's a crucial part of **API** security.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing a shield protecting valuable API services, with icons representing usage tracking and consumption limits.

slides.title: Crafting API Requests
slides.narration:
How do we create an **API** request?
It has essential components.
These include endpoints, headers, and parameters.
Each part tells the **API** what you need.
We'll look at these in more detail.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing distinct components of an API request: endpoints, headers, and parameters, clearly labeled.

slides.title: Processing AI Responses
slides.narration:
Once the **API** sends a response, what happens?
Applications interpret and use this **AI**-generated data.
They might display it, save it, or use it for further processing.
Think about it: the application makes sense of the data.
This completes the request-response cycle.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration of an application receiving and interpreting AI-generated data, showing various ways it might be used (display, save, process).

slides.title: Conceptual API Workflow
slides.narration:
Let's see a conceptual workflow of an **API** interaction.
Imagine your application sending a request.
It goes to the **AI API** for processing.
Then, the **AI API** returns a response.
Notice the clear steps in this full cycle.
This shows how an application gets an **AI** response.
slides.image_prompt: Diagram showing a conceptual workflow: application sending request to AI API, AI API processing, and returning a response.

slides.title: Summary Slide
slides.narration:
Let us summarize what we learned.
We defined **APIs** as software intermediaries.
They are crucial for integrating **AI** models.
We also explored the request-response cycle.
Finally, we understood the role of **API** keys.

slides.title: Assignment Slide
slides.narration:
Now as an assignment,
Think of an app you use that might use an **API**.
Describe how it might send a request and get a response.
Compare the results with a friend.
